## Homework — same notebook, second half

| Wk | Task |
|---|---|
| 1 | Three parts, on the student's OWN birthday, each serving a different takeaway. (1) YOUR OWN BIRTHQUAKE, then your own count — ONE task, because it is one load of one day. Load your birthday and print your birthquake (magnitude, place, depth) with the same max() and .index() move class used on the demo day; the week is called "What was your birthquake?" and a student must not finish it knowing only somebody else's. Then, from the SAME day with the magnitude floor removed entirely, how many earthquakes there were, against a guess committed before looking. The birthquake is the warm-up that proves the load worked; the count is the question. TEMPLATE's "one task per part" is about not stacking unrelated asks, and these are two prints off one day. Serves takeaway 2 and catalogue completeness. (2) The fork: extrapolate the ten-to-one rule down from M4.5 to predict that total, and report how far off it is. Serves takeaway 2. (3) How many days of data do you need before the plate boundaries appear? Map your birthday, your birth week and your birth month, and say which is the first span where the lines show rather than scattered dots — with the earthquake count that took. No single right answer; a defensible one with a number attached. Serves takeaways 3 and 1, which class raises and nothing else at home tests. EVERY PART ENDS IN A QUESTION ANSWERED IN WORDS, in a markdown cell under the self-check, about the numbers that student's own screen printed (TEMPLATE 4). Naming the outputs to produce is not a question: the first version of part 2 said "print the prediction, the count and the ratio" and closed with a hint pointing at an earlier section, so a student could finish it having computed two numbers and thought nothing. Part 1 asks the largest of HOW MANY; part 2 asks which of two readings the overshoot supports and what settles it; part 3 asks which map first shows lines and at what count.
 |
| 2 | Run your function on every planet that has the numbers to support it. Then change the albedo to Venus's and widen the window, and report how many worlds move in and out. Then name one planet your test calls habitable that you do not believe, and say what the test is missing. |
| 3 | How FEW bins before the two peaks merge into one? Find that number for Earth and for Mars, and say which planet holds its two peaks longer. Then weight every cell by cos(latitude) and re-run: the fraction of Earth below sea level moves by about five points. Say which number is the honest one, and what the lon-lat grid was doing to the poles. Then switch containers and group the earthquake catalogue by year. |
| 4 | Colour the earthquakes by depth, then overlay the trenches. Say where the deep events are and why they sit where they do — you are looking at subducting slabs. |
| 5 | Now the forecast: count M6+ near Berkeley, get a rate, and use Poisson for the chance of one during your four years here. Report a single number — week 8 will make you regret that. |
| 6 | Now the seafloor. Fit distance against age for the Pacific-Antarctic Ridge — a free fit puts the ridge 181 km of spreading distance (about 90 km of ocean floor per flank) away from itself at age zero. Force it through the origin, and say why physics required that. |
| 7 | Fit Gutenberg-Richter on M3.5-5.0 in California, predict how many M7+ to expect in 36 years, then count the real ones. Write down whether you think your model failed — you cannot settle it yet. |
| 8 | Then go back to your week-5 answer. You counted events to get a rate, then computed a probability. Bootstrap the rate, and report that probability as an interval instead of a number. |
| 9 | Fit degrees 1 to 9, plot train and test error against degree, and pick a degree with a reason. |
| 10 | Retrain without depth. Explain why the score fell and why the second model is the honest one. |
| 11 | Train a forest on the ten major oxides, then on all 51 columns. More columns wins — 0.965 against 0.921 — and the obvious reading, that the sparse trace elements carry real signal, is WRONG and measurably so: the 19 mostly-empty columns hold 0.097 of the forest's importance and the best ranks 24th, while a forest handed ONLY the pattern of blanks, no measurement at all, scores 0.868 against a 0.343 baseline. Much of the advantage is the compilation remembering which study each sample came from — week 9's leakage, arriving in a week that did not go looking for it. Then delete the imputer and use dropna() instead: the ten oxides leave 271 rows, all 51 leave exactly 1. Say which number you would report to a geochemist, and what you would have concluded from the win alone.
 |
| 12 | Re-run DBSCAN with eps halved and then doubled. Report how many clusters each gives, pick the value you would defend, and then name one cluster you think is a real fault and one you think the algorithm invented. You cannot prove either — say what evidence would settle it. |
| 13 | Final project. |
| 14 | None. The final project is the assessment. |
